children: Second annual global study of 1,100 automotive software developers finds persistent integration challenges, rising security concerns and a more practical view of AI in SDV development
Key Findings from the 2026 Under the Hood: SDV Developer Report:

35% of developer effort is spent, on average, on software integration work below the vehicle application layer rather than building differentiating consumer features with 19% spending at least half their time on that integration work.
76% agree that OEMs should prioritize application-layer innovation over software infrastructure, highlighting the continued importance of focusing on delivering differentiating customer experiences.
75% say the lack of a common, reusable software foundation slows SDV development.
Security is now the number one future concern among developers (48%), and 83% believe SDVs will become a major cyberattack target within the next three years.
AI expectations are becoming more practical: only a quarter think AI will be ‘transformational' (down from 36%), while those seeing it as significant and integrated into workflows rose to 62%.
WATERLOO, ON / ACCESS Newswire / October 21, 2026 /
QNX, a division of BlackBerry Limited
today released its second annual
Under the Hood: SDV Developer Report

, a global study of 1,100 automotive software developers that examines how attitudes towards the software-defined vehicle (SDV) development landscape are evolving as the industry moves from ambition to execution. When it comes to innovation roadblocks, the research found that developers spend an average of 35% of their time on foundational software integration work rather than developing new features and capabilities that differentiate vehicles, while three quarters say the lack of a common, reusable software foundation is slowing overall SDV development.
Software-Defined Delays

The automotive industry is at a critical inflection point, with automakers racing to move faster and ship software more efficiently. Against that backdrop, 79% of developers report feeling pressure from faster-moving competitors, reinforcing the need to balance software development speed and scalability with safety and reliability.

This pressure to go faster however introduces new risks, and software failures are continuing to reshape automotive development practices. Just over half (53%) of automotive software developers are directly influenced by product recalls affecting the industry, with nearly nine in ten (88%) say recalls or failures have led to major or moderate changes in how their teams develop software, suggesting teams are no longer adjusting processes at the margins after an incident, but fundamentally changing how software is architected from the start.
The Need for Application-Layer Innovation

Developers are also clear about where they would rather focus their energy. More than three quarters (76%) agree that OEMs should concentrate on application-layer innovation rather than foundational software infrastructure, the layer where brand identity and customer experience are increasingly defined. That view has softened slightly from 80% in 2025, pointing to a more measured sense of how quickly that shift can happen in practice. When asked what would free their teams up to spend more time on differentiating features, developers almost half (46%) identified better integration across development tools and environments, alongside greater software reuse across vehicle programs (38%), and a pre-integrated foundational software solution (34%). Together, the findings describe an industry that knows where it wants to go but is still getting bogged down in the foundational work beneath.
Delivery is Under Strain

These pressures are showing up in day-to-day software delivery. Debugging and testing is now the single biggest challenge facing automotive software teams, cited by 44% of developers and up eight percentage points year on year, moving ahead of integration complexity (39%) and long development cycles (37%). Perceptions of development environment productivity have also softened, with the share rating their environment as "excellent" falling from 30% to 20%. Taken together, the findings point to teams that are well equipped but increasingly stretched, spending more of their effort finding and fixing problems in foundational layers than ideating, creating and delivering new features that can influence consumer purchase decisions and build brand loyalty.

"The industry is facing a complexity management challenge. Automotive software developers are trying to solve the same integration, software development and safety problems time and time again, and when a third of engineering effort goes into rebuilding software below the application layer, that is a third of the effort not going into the differentiating features drivers actually notice," said Justin Moon, Vice President, Core Product Engineering at QNX. "This year's data shows this approach is beginning to have consequences; debugging has become the biggest challenge developers face, perceptions of productivity are freefalling, and security has moved to the top of the agenda, all of which are symptoms of technical complexity. To reduce that, teams need a trusted software foundation they can build on, certify against and reuse, rather than starting from scratch with every program."
Security and Regulation Move up the Agenda

Looking towards the future, security has moved from a technical consideration to the industry's defining concern. Almost half of developers (48%) now rank security threats as their greatest worry, up five points year over year, while 47% point to cyber vulnerabilities as the biggest risk to rolling out SDVs at scale. More strikingly, 83% expect SDVs to become a ‘major' target for cyberattacks within the next three years, a view that reflects how quickly connectivity and the potential for OTA updates have widened the attack surface. From a regulatory standpoint, cybersecurity standards (ie: UNECE WP.29, ISO/SAE 21434) remain the hardest to meet, cited by 46%, underlining that compliance is no longer a checkbox exercise, but rather, a design constraint shaping architecture decisions from the outset.

Additionally, more than 700 new regulations and legislative proposals affecting in-car technology were introduced globally in 2025 alone, with a third of respondents claiming this has delayed development timelines. With no year-over-year improvement, the data suggests the vast majority of developers haven't yet identified how to efficiently manage the global regulatory burden.
AI: From Hype to Workflow

Expectations of AI have matured rather than cooled. The share of developers describing AI as 'transformational' has fallen from 36% to 25%, while those expecting it to play a significant role integrated into everyday workflows has risen from 55% to 62%. However, 87% still expect AI to have a major role in development but the emphasis has moved from complete reinvention to practical, embedded assistance. That pragmatism suggests an industry moving past the experimentation phase and beginning to judge AI on the same terms as any other tool in the toolchain and whether it measurably shortens the workload in front of them.

"The industry has spent several years talking about SDVs as a design ambition, but as the data shows, resources during that time have been concentrated on the middleware layer," said Maite Bezerra, Senior Principal Analyst at Omdia. "When teams exhaust resources building custom infrastructure instead of standardizing foundational layers, they miss the point. Innovation in middleware is not only challenging for companies that aren't software-first, but it also doesn't drive direct customer value. Until automakers step away from the plumbing and focus on the application layer, they will continue to lack a solid business case for SDVs."
